In sum, in analyzing intraindividual variability using the RI-CLPM, we are interested in assessing how changes in one time-varying variable are associated with changes in another time-varying variable at the following time point, after controlling for the (in)stability of the former variable.

Choosing Between MLM and SEM

Following our review of MLM and SEM approaches to examine intraindividual change and variability, we briefly describe a few considerations that may help researchers choose between using the MLM or SEM framework. One of the primary distinctions between these two frameworks is their (in)ability to incorporate measurement error -i.e., the extent of unreliability in the measures. A major advantage of SEM is that it allows for explicit modeling of measurement error. SEMs specify latent constructs (i.e., factors) that are informed by multiple observed indicators using a measurement model, which ideally enables the separation of true score variance from random error variance in the measures and results in unbiased estimates of model parameters (Curran 2003). In contrast, MLMs take the observed variables as directly representing the constructs of interest, without parsing measurement error. Despite not considering measurement error, the use of MLM may be apt when a study design uses singleitem measures, as is often the case in experience sampling studies, because there is no measurement model to fit.

The MLM and SEM frameworks also differ in their flexibility with unbalanced data.

Repeated assessments often result in datasets with missing values and differing numbers of observations across participants. A major advantage of MLM is its ability to accurately estimate parameters even with missing data and uneven assessment intervals across participants (Curran 2003). In contrast, SEM requires relatively balanced data (i.e., little missing data, equal intervals between measurement occasions) to correctly estimate the model (Curran 2003). This limitation is especially relevant in the context of experience sampling studies that come with a higher number of repeated measurements and a higher likelihood of missing data. Balanced data may be more attainable with fewer measurement occasions.

The ability to assess model fit also differs across frameworks. In SEM, the overall model fit is evaluated using global fit indices that assess the extent to which the estimated model fits the actual data (Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016). In contrast, MLM fit assessment occurs by way of model comparison rather than through global fit indices (Barr et al. 2013). Specifically, model comparison in the MLM framework examines whether nested models (e.g., comparing a model with a random intercept to a model with a random intercept and random slope) exhibit significant improvement (i.e., decrease) in model prediction error (e.g., by examining Akaike Information one model fits better than a similar model, they do not assess whether the overall fit is good.

Criterion and Bayesian Information Criterion values). Although these values indicate whether

Finally, these two frameworks differ in terms of model specification and complexity.

SEM allows for the examination of more complex relationships among variables, such as addressing questions of longitudinal mediation (e.g., Bollen 1987) or the relation of predictors to multiple outcomes (Curran 2003). While MLM cannot as easily examine mediation or multivariate outcomes, it does accommodate data with multiple levels of nesting, such as following children in a school over time across the country (i.e., time points nested within children, nested within classroom, nested within school).

In summary, considerations such as measurement error, unbalanced data, and model evaluation and complexity are critical when choosing between SEM and MLM frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data. To help make the choice and interpretation of these models more concrete, we next illustrate how to examine intraindividual change and variability with an example from an intensive longitudinal project centered on mobile technology and daily mobility (Mao et al. 2023; Ross et al. 2023; see the OSF pagefoot_2 for more information).

Empirical Example

We examine the relationship between social app usage and the desire to interact, as well as daily changes in the desire for social interaction. To do so, we leverage data from Project mCog, which combined daily repeated self-report surveys with passive sensing of app log data.

Prior studies have explored the role of different types of social media and mobile phone use on individuals' social lives. Moreover, research has shown that individuals use a variety of mobile communication channels (e.g., social media, call, text) to satisfy their need to connect with their close ties (Hall 2023; Hall and Miller 2023). However, fewer studies have investigated the impact of mobile communication on face-to-face interpersonal interactions (e.g., Hall and Miller 2023) -or the desire to interact in-person specifically. Therefore, we investigate the relationship between mobile social app use -specifically, social media use and messaging use -and the desire to interact in "real-life".

Before examining the impact of mobile communication on the desire for social interaction, we first explore intraindividual changes in individuals' desire to socially interact over the course of the day to better understand individuals' social interaction cycles (Warner 1988). Specifically, following Ross et al. (2023), we examined whether individuals' desire to socially interact follows a quadratic (inverted-U) trend over the course of a day. In other words, we test whether an individual's desire to socially interact initially increases, peaks during the middle of the day, and then decreases toward the end of the day. As such, our research question about intraindividual change in desire to socially interact is:

RQ1: Do intraindividual changes in individuals' desire to socially interact follow a quadratic (inverted-U) trend over the course of a day?

We next examine intraindividual variability in individuals' desire to socially interact throughout the day as a function of their social app use. We predict that once individuals' social needs are met through social platforms, they will have a reduced desire to socially interact faceto-face. As such, our first research hypothesis regarding intraindividual variability is:

H1: There is a negative association between recent social app use and individuals' desire to socially interact.

We further explore the moderating role of extraversion on the relationship between social app use and the desire to socially interact (Bowden-Green, Hinds, and Joinson 2020):

H2: The association between recent social app use and individuals' desire to socially interact will be weaker for individuals higher in extraversion than for individuals lower in extraversion.

We tested our hypotheses using the MLM framework due to its flexibility with unbalanced data and our use of single-item measures for our primary study variables (i.e., we cannot incorporate a measurement model and measurement error).

Procedure

Prior to the start of the experience sampling and mobile sensing phase, participants were asked to complete a baseline survey that consisted of demographic and Big Five personality questionnaires. During the following two weeks, participants used the study application to complete up to six brief surveys per day. For each survey, participants self-reported their in vivo emotional valence, arousal level, energy level, and desire for social interaction (as well as questions tied to specific studies within the broader project). By default, surveys were sent at random times within six equal time intervals across the day. However, surveys could also be triggered if a participant engaged in walking (given the broader goals of the project to study daily mobility), which replaced one of the six random surveys. These intervals were created based on the wake and sleep times that participants configured in the study application. The study application also recorded whether the participant's smartphone screen was on or off, as well as the foreground app on the screen every (up to ten seconds). After two weeks, participants completed an endpoint survey. Participants who completed all parts of the study received $95.

Overall, participants completed 29,507 experience sampling surveys (~69 surveys per participant; 6,445 missing in total) and contributed logs of their smartphone app use (n = 12,622,401 instances of app use recorded on the foreground; n = 2,119,176 instances of social media app use; n = 1,431,199 instances of messaging app use).

Measures

We drew from the baseline survey to assess extraversion, from the experience sampling surveys to assess desire to interact, and from the app log data to determine social app use.

Descriptive statistics for the key study variables can be found in Table 1.

Extraversion

We measured individuals' extraversion from four items collected as part of a scale measuring the Big Five personality traits -specifically, the 20-item version of the International Personality Item Pool (Donnellan et al. 2006). Participants were asked to evaluate the extent to which four items (e.g., "I am the life of the party", "I don't talk a lot") accurately describe their behavior, using a five-point scale ranging from "Very inaccurate" (1) to "Very accurate" (5). We centered extraversion around the sample mean to facilitate interpretation.

Desire to Interact

We measured the desire to interact with one item in every experience sampling survey: "Right now, do you want to be alone or with other people?"

Participants rated their desire to socially interact on a five-point scale from "I only want to be alone" (1) to "I only want to be with other people" (5).

Social App Use

We focused on messaging and social media apps from our list of validated apps (for a detailed description of the app validation procedure, see Ross et al. 2023). Social media and messaging apps were largely operationalized based on the Google Play Store categories of "social" and "communication", respectively. Based on these social media and messaging apps, we calculated binary measures of social media and messaging app use. Specifically, app use consisted of whether a social media or messaging app was recorded in the foreground of participants' screens in the 60 minutes prior to answering an experience sampling survey.

Overall, 16,461 (58%) occasions of social media use and 15,187 (53%) occasions of messaging app use were recorded prior to a survey. We person-mean centered individuals' social media and messaging app use to separate interindividual differences from intraindividual variability, and we included both components in our model examining intraindividual variability. We operationalized time based on the chronological order of when the study app prompted participants to complete their experience sampling surveys each day. As individuals received prompts six times a day, the surveys were coded from 1 to 6. Additionally, since we speculated a quadratic (inverted-U) change in the desire to socially interact, we centered time to reduce collinearity between the linear and quadratic components of the growth model (Biesanz et al. 2004).

Analytic Procedure: Intraindividual Change

We used an MLM to examine how an individual's desire to socially interact changed over the course of a day. For the sake of model simplicity, we only examined curvilinear changes in the desire to socially interact during the first study day for each individual (i.e., to avoid adding another level that represented the day to the MLM). Specifically, 2,107 experience sampling surveys nested within 428 individuals were used to fit a curvilinear (U-shaped) growth model and modeled as: where 𝛽 0𝑖 represents the expected value of the desire to socially interact at the first experience sampling survey of the day for individual i; 𝛽 1𝑖 represents the expected amount of linear change in the desire to socially interact for individual i across a day; 𝛽 2𝑖 is the expected quadratic change in the desire to socially interact for individual i across a day; and residuals (𝑒 𝑖𝑡 ) account for unexplained variance in the outcome for individual i across all time points.

To account for variability in the intercept and slopes between individuals, the Level 2 equations are: where 𝛾 00 is the prototypical (i.e., grand mean) desire to socially interact for individual i at the first experience sampling survey of the day, and 𝑢 0𝑖 is the deviation of each individual i's desire to socially interact from the grand mean.

Likewise, 𝛾 10 is the prototypical linear growth in the desire to socially interact for individual i, and 𝑢 1𝑖 is the deviation of each individual i's linear slope in the desire to socially interact from the prototypical linear change. Finally, 𝛾 20 is the prototypical quadratic change in the desire to socially interact across all individuals in the sample. 4 The random effects are assumed to be multivariate normally distributed.

Analytic Procedure: Intraindividual Variability

We used two MLMs to examine how the fluctuations in social app (social media, messaging) use might affect individuals' desire to socially interact. Specifically, 29,507 experience sampling surveys nested within 428 individuals were modeled at Level 1 as: where 𝐷𝑒𝑠𝑖𝑟𝑒 𝑡𝑜 𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑎𝑐𝑡 𝑖𝑡 is the reported desire to socially interact for individual i at experience sampling survey t; 𝛽 0𝑖 is the average level of an individual i's desire to socially interact; 𝛽 1𝑖 is the association between an individual i's desire to socially interact and their state social app use; and 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 are individual-specific residuals that represent the unexplained variability in an individual's desire to socially interact at each time point that is not captured by social app use and that are assumed to be normally distributed.

Interindividual differences were modeled at Level 2 as: where 𝛾 00 is the prototypical level of an individual's desire to socially interact; 𝛾 01 is the prototypical association between an individual i's trait social app use and their desire to socially interact; 𝛾 02 is the prototypical association between an individual i's extraversion and their desire to socially interact; 𝑢 0𝑖 represents the deviation of each individual i from the prototypical level of the desire to socially interact; 𝛾 10 is the prototypical effect of an individual's state social app use on their desire to socially interact; 𝛾 11 represents how individuals' trait social app use moderates the association between state social app use on their desire to socially interact; 𝛾 12 represents how extraversion moderates the association between state social app use and the desire to socially interact; and 𝑢 1𝑖 represents the deviation of each individual i from the prototypical association between state social app use and the desire to socially interact.

We included the random effects in our model to account for the heterogeneity of social media effects on individuals (e.g., Meier and Reinecke 2021).

MLM models were fit to the data in R (R Core Team 2023) using the lmer library (Bates et al. 2015). Incomplete data were treated as missing at random, and statistical significance was evaluated at p < .05. The data and code for these analyses can be found on OSF 5.

Results

Intraindividual change

Results from the growth model examining intraindividual changes in the desire to socially interact across a day (day 1 of sampling across all participants) are shown in Table 2. As expected, the quadratic model provided the best (of the models fit) representation of the data (as indicated by the lowest AIC and BIC when compared to models with no change and linear trajectories of growth; see supplemental materials on OSF for these model comparisons). We found that the desire to socially interact exhibited a significant inverted-U change over the course of a day ( γ20 = -0.02, p < .001). Furthermore, we found significant interindividual differences in the initial level of the desire to socially interact (σ𝑢0 = 0.50, CI: [0.45, 0.56]). In other words, individuals significantly differed in their typical inclination to socially interact at the middle of the day. Additionally, there were interindividual differences in the linear change of the desire to socially interact (σ𝑢1 = 0.20, CI: [0.17, 0.23]), which indicates heterogeneity across individuals in the linear growth component of the desire to socially interact.

In sum, we found that the desire for social interaction shows quadratic change over the course of a day, addressing RQ1. Our data revealed that participants' desire to engage in social interactions might be linked to circadian rhythms and daily cycles of activity and rest (Warren 1988), such that the individuals' reports of their desire to socially interact started out relatively low in the morning upon waking, steadily increased through the midday hours, peaking in the late afternoon before declining again in the evening hours leading up to typical bedtimes.

Intraindividual variability

Table 3 contains the results from the two MLMs examining the relationship between changes in social app use and changes in individuals' desire to socially interact. As expected, the MLM with a random intercept and slope provided the best (of the models fit) representation of the social media app use data (as indicated by the lowest AIC and BIC) when it was compared to models with no random intercept and slope. Model fit was not different between the random intercept only and random intercept and slope models for the messaging app use model, but we We conclude that our hypotheses (H1 and H2) were not supported: social app use in the prior 60 minutes was not associated with individuals' desire to socially interact, and extraversion did not moderate this association. Our results suggest that social app use may not fully satisfy social needs -at least in terms of reducing motives for interacting in-person.

Extensions of Multilevel and Structural Equation Models

We described linear change and associations using MLM and SEM. These analytic frameworks also allow researchers to examine more complex and nonlinear change processes as well as accommodate non-continuous and non-normal data. We next briefly introduce further opportunities that may be relevant for researchers analyzing longitudinal data.

Table 4 provides a summary of and resources for more complex models that can be fit in the MLM and/or SEM framework. For example, researchers may be interested in examining nonlinear change processes, such as the process of mobile media habit formation over a one month period (Schnauber-Stockmann & Naab, 2019). These types of nonlinear models extend the linear growth models described previously by including additional parameters that capture curvature or knot points in the growth trajectory (Grimm et al. 2013). Furthermore, researchers can identify whether different subgroups exhibit distinct change processes using growth mixture models (Grimm et al. 2013; Ram and Grimm 2009). For instance, researchers have explored different trajectories of parent-child sex-communication, with subgroups of parents having safesex conversations with their adolescents before the age of 16, some having conversations after the age of 16, and the majority having conversations between 14 and 18 years of age (Padilla-Walker, Rogers, and McLean 2020).

Researchers may also want to expand their analyses by examining multiple outcomes simultaneously (MacCallum et al. 1997), such as reciprocal processes of anger and conflict in the parent-adolescent relationship from day to day (LoBraico et al. 2020). Alternatively, researchers may be interested in incorporating mediators or moderators into their model (Bolger and Laurenceau 2013; Peng, Zhang, and Wang 2021; Selig and Preacher 2009; Wittenberg et al. 2019). For example, researchers have examined the mediating role of different motives on the association between individuals' perception of autonomy and their addiction to social networking sites (Masur et al. 2014). Multilevel structural equation models (Christ et al. 2017; Kroencke et al. 2023; Preacher, Zyphur, and Zhang 2010) may be especially useful for fitting these models as they can simultaneously handle complex processes (e.g., mediation, multivariate outcomes) and data structures (e.g., unbalanced data).

Finally, researchers may work with outcome variables that are not normally distributed.

Outcome variables may be non-normal due to their measurement (e.g., binary, categorical) or due to how the process manifests (e.g., low occurrence, skewed distribution). For example, researchers have explored whether smartphone use (versus non-use), a binary outcome variable, is associated with being in certain places or certain social situations (Roehrick, Vaid, and Harari 2023). To accommodate this non-normal outcome, the researchers fit hurdle models to account for many zeros in the outcome while simultaneously modeling the non-zero values. In sum, MLMs and SEMs serve as a flexible foundation on which researchers can build more complex longitudinal models that capture their change processes of interest. Examine nonlinear trajectories of growth/decay, such as trajectories that have a flexible functional form or differ based on distinct segments of time (Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016).

Underlying groups E.g., growth mixture models Identify subgroups of individuals that share similar underlying change trajectories when the grouping variable is not explicitly measured and predicted a priori (see Grimm et al. 2013; Ram and Grimm 2009).

Complex change processes

Mediation E.g., within-person mediation Identify the mechanism through which the independent variable influences the dependent variable over time.

For between-subject mediation analysis, see Cole and Maxwell (2003).

For within-subject mediation analysis, see Bolger and Laurenceau (2013).

For cross-level mediation, see Krull and MacKinnon (2001).

For multilevel structural equation models, see Christ et al. (2017); Preacher, Zyphur, and Zhang (2010). For within-subject moderation analysis, see Barr (2013); Bauer and Curran (2005); Bolger and Laurenceau (2013).

Multivariate processes E.g., dyadic models Examine intraindividual change/variability when there is more than one outcome (Bolger and Laurenceau 2013; MacCallum et al. 1997).

Different types of outcomes

Non-continuous data E.g., categorical outcomes, binary outcomes Examine intraindividual change/variability when the outcome is not continuous, oftentimes through link functions (logit and probit link functions) connecting the non-continuous dependent variable with the continuous independent variables (Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016).

Non-normal data E.g., zero-inflated models Examine intraindividual change/variability when the outcome is not normally distributed (e.g., zero-inflated Poisson or zero-inflated negative binomial distributions are used when the proportion of 0 responses is higher than other response categories; see Grimm, Ram, and Estabrook 2016).

Conclusion

In this chapter, we introduced MLM and SEM frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data in communication research. Within these frameworks, we focused on capturing two major types of change processes: (1) intraindividual change, which manifests as directional growth or decay trajectories within an individual, and (2) intraindividual variability, which manifests as fluctuations around an equilibrium within an individual. By illustrating the examination of these two change processes using an intensive longitudinal experience sampling and mobile tracking study, we hope researchers see how these models can be implemented in practice and applied to their own research questions. There is a large range of approaches available to examine change processes (see Brinberg and Lydon-Staley 2023), and we hope this chapter serves as a springboard for researchers looking to incorporate these techniques into their own toolkits.

ParticipantsA

Participants were 35.3 years old on average and 65% identified as female. Participants were recruited on Facebook and Instagram from the local metropolitan area (Columbus, Ohio, USA), and via a random survey of students from The Ohio State University. To meet eligibility requirements, potential participants had to (a) be at least 18 years old, (b) have a US phone number, and (c) possess an Android smartphone capable of running the study application. We excluded participants (n = 37) who did not complete at least half of the surveys and who had log data missing for at least half of the hours during the study period. Our final sample used for analysis consisted of N = 428 participants.

Contrary to our hypothesis, we did not find any significant association between recent social app use and individuals' desire to socially interact (social media app use: γ10 = 0.07, p = 0.10; messaging app use: γ10 = 0.04, p = 0.27). Furthermore, while individuals' reports of extraversion were significantly and positively associated with their desire to socially interact (γ02 = 0.11, p < 0.001), extraversion did not moderate the relationship between the desire to socially interact and social app use (social media app use: γ10 = 0.01, p = 0.34; messaging app use: γ10 = 0.01, p = 0.52). Finally, we found significant interindividual differences in individuals' prototypical social app use (social media app use: σ𝑢0 = 0.46, CI: [0.43, 0.49]; messaging app use: σ𝑢0 = 0.46, CI: [0.43, 0.49]). We also found significant interindividual differences in the strength of the association between social app use and the desire to socially interact (social media app use: σ𝑢1 = 0.12, CI: [0.07, 0.16]; messaging app use: σ𝑢1 = 0.06, CI: [0.00, 0.11]), indicating heterogeneity in the association between social app use and the desire to socially interact among individuals in the sample.

Bios

Razieh Pourafshari (M.A., University of Tehran) is a PhD student in the School of Communication at The Ohio State University. Her research revolves around how and when digital communication enhances or undermines feelings of connection between people. Using intensive longitudinal methods and dyadic analysis, her work explores technology use as a dynamic, relational process operating across time, partners, and contexts. Miriam Brinberg (PhD, Pennsylvania State University) is an Assistant Professor in the School of Communication at The Ohio State University. Her research focuses on examining interpersonal interactions in everyday life and developing methods to better understand those interactions. Joseph (Joe) Bayer (PhD, University of Michigan) is an Associate Professor based in the School of Communication and affiliated with the Translational Data Analytics Institute (TDAI) and Department of Psychology at The Ohio State University. He directs the Mobile Social Cognition Lab, which combines digital trace and ecological survey methods to study the mental processes that underlie social connection. In turn, his research grapples with how our minds are changing due to smartphone and social media habits, along with the implications for digital wellbeing and addictive behavior.
